title: Wisconsin's Oldest Known Cemetery Site Lies Beside the Oconto River
summary: Copper Culture State Park preserves a prehistoric cemetery associated with the Old Copper Complex, whose people occupied the northern Midwest thousands of years ago. The DNR describes the burial ground as Wisconsin's oldest cemetery site and possibly the oldest in eastern North America.
location: Copper Culture State Park, Oconto County

title: Ancient Copper Workers Lived Along the Oconto River Thousands of Years Ago
summary: Long before European settlement, Old Copper Complex people occupied northeastern Wisconsin and worked native copper into tools and other objects. A major cemetery connected to that culture survives at today's Copper Culture State Park.
location: Copper Culture State Park, Oconto County

title: The Ancient Oconto Burials Are Connected to Menominee Ancestors
summary: Modern archaeological interpretation identifies the people buried at the Oconto Site as direct prehistoric ancestors of the Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin, connecting one of the state's oldest archaeological sites with a living Wisconsin nation.
location: Copper Culture State Park, Oconto County

title: Wisconsin's Oldest Standing Logging Camp Still Sits Where It Was Built
summary: Holt and Balcom Logging Camp No. 1 was built in 1880 and remains on its original site east of Lakewood. The Wisconsin Historical Society identifies its bunkhouse as the oldest known logging-camp building in Wisconsin still standing where it was constructed.

title: An 1880 Logging Camp Had a Cookhouse, Bunkhouse and Open Dogtrot
summary: Holt and Balcom's surviving camp building was built from round white-pine logs and divided by a twelve-foot open breezeway. One side served as the cookhouse while the other held double-deck bunks for logging crews.

title: A Northwoods Logging Camp Once Included Its Own Blacksmith Shop and Farm Fields
summary: The Holt and Balcom camp was once a small self-contained settlement in the woods. Besides its surviving cookhouse and bunkhouse, the operation included a blacksmith shop, horse barn, warehouse, truck garden, pasture and hay fields.

title: The Peshtigo Fire Obliterated Towns in Only Hours
summary: On October 8, 1871, a firestorm swept across northeastern Wisconsin and virtually destroyed Peshtigo. The Wisconsin Historical Society records more than 1,100 known deaths, with hundreds more believed killed, making it the deadliest forest fire in American history.

title: The Peshtigo Fire Burned a Swath Roughly 10 Miles Wide and 40 Miles Long
summary: The 1871 Peshtigo Fire tore through a massive corridor of northeastern Wisconsin. Historical Society accounts describe a devastated swath about ten miles wide and forty miles long, with flames spreading across multiple counties.

title: Thousands Were Left Homeless by the Peshtigo Fire
summary: Beyond the enormous death toll, the Peshtigo Fire created a humanitarian disaster across northeastern Wisconsin. Thousands of survivors were left homeless and many more suffered serious injuries after the firestorm passed.

title: Peshtigo's Residents Had Grown Used to the Smell of Smoke Before Disaster Struck
summary: Drought had left the Peshtigo region dangerously dry for weeks before October 8, 1871. Residents had become so accustomed to smoke and ash from surrounding fires that many went to bed without realizing the catastrophe that was approaching.

title: Peshtigo Was a Lumber Powerhouse Before the Fire
summary: Immediately before the famous fire, Peshtigo was a thriving lumber town. Its harbor mill could produce roughly 150,000 feet of lumber per day, while other local mills manufactured doors, window sash and blinds.

title: The Peshtigo Fire Burned the Same Night as the Great Chicago Fire
summary: Peshtigo burned on October 8, 1871—the same night as the Great Chicago Fire. News of Chicago's disaster traveled quickly, while the catastrophe in rural northeastern Wisconsin initially received far less attention despite its far greater death toll.

title: The Peshtigo Fire Burned Across More Than a Quarter-Million Acres
summary: The fire complex associated with the Peshtigo disaster burned more than 280,000 acres across northeastern Wisconsin, affecting communities and forests in Marinette, Oconto, Shawano, Brown, Kewaunee, Door, Manitowoc and Outagamie counties.

title: Northern Wisconsin Was Marketed to Farmers After Loggers Cut the Forests
summary: As northern Wisconsin's great pine forests disappeared, state leaders expected farms to replace them. In 1895 the Legislature directed the University of Wisconsin's College of Agriculture to create a 200-page handbook encouraging settlers to establish homesteads on the cutover lands.

title: University Researchers Crossed Northern Wisconsin Photographing Life for Homesteaders
summary: To produce Wisconsin's official handbook for prospective northern settlers, University of Wisconsin staff traveled across the region in 1895 taking photographs and documenting farms, crops and the opportunities they believed existed on recently logged land.

title: Native Encampments Once Occupied Today's Council Grounds State Park
summary: The Wisconsin River site now protected as Council Grounds State Park near Merrill was once used for Native American encampments. The park's name preserves the area's long association with gatherings along the river.
location: Council Grounds State Park, Lincoln County

title: Ancient Hunters Followed Retreating Glaciers Through the Amnicon Country
summary: After the last great glacier began retreating from northern Wisconsin, nomadic hunters moved through the Amnicon River country. DNR history places people hunting mastodons in this landscape about 9,000 years ago.
location: Amnicon Falls State Park, Douglas County

title: Ancient Copper Workers Searched the Amnicon River's Rocks
summary: Old Copper Culture people occupied the western Lake Superior region for thousands of years. Around today's Amnicon Falls State Park, they searched rocky outcrops for native copper that could be worked into tools.
location: Amnicon Falls State Park, Douglas County

title: Copper Prospectors Dug Around Amnicon Falls—and Mostly Failed
summary: European-American prospectors moved into the Amnicon Falls area during the 1850s hoping its geology concealed valuable copper deposits. Most attempts failed, but traces of their searches remain visible in the park landscape.
location: Amnicon Falls State Park, Douglas County

title: A Railroad Company Once Owned the Land Around Amnicon Falls
summary: To encourage railroad construction through northern Wisconsin, the state transferred large blocks of federal land to railroad companies. The property around today's Amnicon Falls State Park became part of land granted to the Chicago, St. Paul, Minneapolis and Omaha Railway.
location: Amnicon Falls State Park, Douglas County

title: A Superior Pioneer Bought the Amnicon Falls in 1886
summary: James Bardon, an early Superior businessman, purchased 160 acres surrounding the Amnicon River waterfalls in 1886 after railroad-grant lands in the region were sold to raise construction money.
location: Amnicon Falls State Park, Douglas County

title: A Pond at Amnicon Falls Is Actually an Abandoned Brownstone Quarry
summary: A quiet pond beside today's Thimbleberry Nature Trail hides an industrial past: it occupies the site of a former brownstone quarry, one remnant of the extraction industries that operated around the Amnicon River.
location: Amnicon Falls State Park, Douglas County

title: Big Manitou Falls Was Nearly Destroyed by a Hydroelectric Dam
summary: In 1917 a proposed hydroelectric project threatened to submerge Big Manitou Falls. Wealthy lumberman and miner Martin Pattison quietly began purchasing hundreds of acres around the Black River to stop the development.

title: Martin Pattison Secretly Bought 660 Acres to Save a Waterfall
summary: Rather than publicly fight plans for a dam, Martin Pattison quietly bought 660 acres from multiple landowners surrounding Big Manitou Falls. He then donated the property to Wisconsin, permanently protecting the waterfall.

title: One Man's Land Donation Created Wisconsin's Sixth State Park
summary: Martin Pattison's donation of land around Big Manitou Falls led Wisconsin to establish Pattison State Park on January 20, 1920. It became the sixth park in the young Wisconsin state park system.

title: Wisconsin's Highest Waterfall Drops 165 Feet Here
summary: Big Manitou Falls plunges 165 feet through the Black River gorge at Pattison State Park. The DNR identifies it as Wisconsin's highest waterfall and the fourth-highest waterfall east of the Rocky Mountains.

title: Ancient People Quarried Quartz Beside Big Manitou Falls
summary: Native people quarried conglomerate near Big Manitou Falls to obtain fist-sized quartz stones. They carried the quartz above the falls and flaked it into knives, spear points and other tools.

title: Big Manitou Falls Was a Gathering Place Long Before It Became a Park
summary: The Big Manitou Falls area was an important landmark and gathering place for Ojibwe people. DNR history reports that a trading post was located at the falls during the nineteenth century.

title: A Surveyor Found Evidence of Ancient Copper Mining Near Little Manitou Falls
summary: Surveyor G. R. Stuntz found a broken stone hammer and work areas near Little Manitou Falls where Native people had mined and shaped copper. The evidence documented metalworking here long before nineteenth-century prospectors arrived.

title: Wisconsin's First Recorded Northwestern Copper Rush Started Below Big Manitou Falls
summary: The first recorded European-American copper exploration in northwestern Wisconsin occurred below Big Manitou Falls and along Copper Creek in 1845–47. Prospectors dug crude openings but abandoned the effort because of poor transportation, limited mining skill and disappointing results.

title: Civil War Demand Triggered 'Copper Fever' in Douglas County
summary: Rising copper demand during the Civil War revived mining dreams in Douglas County. Experienced miners arrived from Michigan, promising assay reports circulated, and what DNR history calls 'copper fever' spread across the region.

title: Old Mine Shafts Still Hide Around Pattison State Park
summary: Repeated attempts to find profitable copper left test holes, trenches, tunnels and shafts scattered around Pattison State Park. A triangular opening at the base of Big Manitou Falls and a shallow cave near Little Manitou Falls remain evidence of the failed mining rushes.

title: Martin Pattison Logged the Black River Before He Saved Its Famous Falls
locationAccuracy: Black River near Pattison State Park
summary: Decades before donating the land for Pattison State Park, Martin Pattison's company logged along the Black River. His crews operated a camp upstream of Little Manitou Falls for about three years, and remnants survive along today's Logging Camp Trail.

title: Copper Falls Was Mined During the Civil War Era
summary: Prospectors searched the Bad River gorge between Copper Falls and Brownstone Falls for copper during the early 1860s. Early maps show shafts in the canyon, likely connected to increased demand for copper during the Civil War.
location: Copper Falls State Park, Ashland County

title: Ancient Copper Miners Worked the Country Around Copper Falls
summary: Long before nineteenth-century prospectors arrived, Old Copper Culture people mined native copper veins in the region around today's Copper Falls State Park and fashioned the metal into tools and hunting equipment.
location: Copper Falls State Park, Ashland County

title: Early Northern Wisconsin Tanneries Devoured Hemlock Bark
summary: Tanneries flourished in northeastern Wisconsin because hemlock bark supplied tannins needed to process leather. The first tannery in Two Rivers opened in 1850, beginning nearly four decades of intensive local leather production.

title: A Trading Post at 'Mink River' Predated Modern Two Rivers Settlement
summary: Peter Rowley arrived from Ohio in 1835 and established a trading post near today's Point Beach State Forest to trade with Ottawa and Potawatomi people. He called the area Mink River; later surveyors named nearby Rowley Point after him.

title: Government Surveyors Renamed Mink River After Its Early Trader
summary: When government surveyors reached the Lake Michigan shore in 1841, they apparently did not know Peter Rowley's earlier name 'Mink River.' They labeled the landmark Rowley Point after him; the spelling later changed to Rawley Point.

title: Wisconsin's Early Park Builders Left Rustic Stonework Across the State
summary: Civilian Conservation Corps crews transformed Wisconsin state parks during the Depression, constructing ranger stations, cabins, retaining walls, stone stairways and other rustic features. Many of those structures remain in use today.

title: The White-Pine Boom Virtually Stripped Northern Wisconsin's Great Forests
summary: During the second half of the nineteenth century, lumber companies poured into Wisconsin's northern pinery to supply wood for rapidly growing Midwestern farms and cities. The boom eventually removed most of the region's old white-pine forest.

title: Holt and Balcom Owned About a Thousand Acres of Northwoods Timber
summary: Holt and Balcom was one of many firms that converted northeastern Wisconsin's pine forests into lumber. The company controlled roughly a thousand acres in Oconto and Marinette counties and supported crews from isolated camps in the woods.
